2d French Armored Division under the Seventh Army (6th Army Group) from 29 September 1944, when the XV Corps with the division passed to the 6th Army Group and the Seventh Army (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 254). From 5 to 27 December 1944 the First French Army held operational control of the division while the Seventh Army continued to provide its logistical support (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 464), so this standing relation is kept through December; Devers returned the division to the Seventh Army by the letter of instructions of 28 December (p. 496, note 7). The end is an inferred value: no source read dates it. During the January 1945 German offensive the division returned to the XV Corps in the Sarre valley (p. 501) and was then moved south toward Strasbourg for the Colmar offensive (p. 535), but these moves are not dated in the pages read; the interval ends the day before the next row (8 February 1945), with the last row that lists it as the earliest end. Changed in the French follow-up: valid_to was 1945-02-07 (inferred from the next row, earliest end 1944-11-28); it is now 1944-12-04, the day before Devers transferred operational control of the division from the Seventh to the First French Army effective 5 December 1944 (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 464). The division was then attached to the French II Corps (p. 486), returned to the Seventh Army on 28 December (p. 496) and served with the XV Corps in January (p. 501), not with the VI Corps.

French follow-up: Patch moved the whole 2d French Armored Division north to the Sarre River valley to bolster Haislip's XV Corps, where it formed the corps reserve (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 501); elements supported the XV Corps counterattacks after the German offensive of 1 January (p. 505). No source read dates the move, so valid_from is the date of the row that lists it; the end is an inferred value, the day before the next row (28 January 1945). Kind attached, by analogy with the earlier XV Corps attachments. Changed in the de Lattre pass: valid_to was 1945-01-27 (inferred, end unknown); it is now 1945-01-18, the day before the combat commands Dio and Langlade left the US Seventh Army on 19 January (de Lattre, p. 373). de Lattre (p. 331) places the division around Obernai-Marlenheim under the Seventh Army in January, which differs from the Sarre valley of CMH p. 501; not reconciled (the de Lattre quote is truncated, so it is not used for a row).

Six companies of stoottroepen raised at Eindhoven on the day of its liberation are placed at the disposal of XXX Corps and accepted by Horrocks after Prince Bernhard's intervention (de Jong, Het Koninkrijk, deel 10a, pp. 542-545). Kind unspecified_subordination (placed at the disposal of / accepted by). De Jong does not date the end; the interval is left open at the last linked claim. Added in the de Jong 10a-1 follow-up, branch dejong-10a1, 12 November 2026, approved by Scott: old value none, new value this relation. Review (Stoottroepen parent pass, branch small-fixes-1113, 14 November 2026, approved by Scott): C9384 parent_unit_id old value: blank; new value: UK-COR-030C (same day's placement; last_listed_date remains 1944-09-18). Later claims C9385-C9388 were re-read and left with blank parent: C9385 is Limburg recruitment under van Kooten after Bernhard's appointment, not an XXX Corps listing; C9386 is the formal BS organisation (van Houten appoints Borghouts commander of the Stoottroepen der BS south of the great rivers); C9387 says the Eindhoven-area OD stoottroepen, who had at first helped cover the flanks of XXX Corps, were also used at the end of October at the Peel, which is not used to extend last_listed; C9388 is a London war-department strength return for early May 1945 and names no Allied parent. No end date is invented (valid_to_basis remains open_at_last_claim). A second family, Lodders and Kraandijk, '50 jaar regiment Stoottroepen', Militaire Spectator 163 (1994) no. 9 (R1162), records that Commando Limburg, by its direct relationship with the Americans, took increasing distance from Commando Zuid and Brabant (p. 405); the Limburg battalions were employed alongside the Americans from shortly after their formation and came under the Koninklijke landmacht section of Prince Bernhard's staff on 2 January 1945 (p. 406); the English employed Brabant companies as combat units at the front from 11 October 1944, and an English army commander delayed the Brabant transfer into the Koninklijke landmacht until May 1945 (Limburg had transferred in January; Commando Zuid was then abolished) (pp. 405-409). Those passages confirm a split, not a single later Allied parent for NL-INF-STOOT as a whole, and they do not name a numbered British or US army, corps, or army group as a dated superior of the formation. Other opened pages (Veteraneninstituut; stoottroepers.nl; English Wikipedia) are consistent with that split (Limburg under American command or embedded in the US Army; Brabant under British command, or belonging to 21st Army Group on the regimental site) but are not used to invent a formation-level relation. The NIMH article 'De Stoottroepen in oktober 1944' (URL 404 on 14 November 2026) was not opened and is not cited. Stacey and the Dutch Defence canon were searched and do not name a later superior for this unit. Prince Bernhard's Binnenlandse Strijdkrachten is the administrative superior from the 22 September organisation onward, but it is not in the dataset as a unit and is not entered as parent_unit_id.

The Stoottroepen der Binnenlandse Strijdkrachten are the combat arm of the BS, organised in the split of the BS south of the great rivers on 22 September 1944 (de Jong, Het Koninkrijk, deel 10a, pp. 561-563, R894; NIMH, De oprichting van de Binnenlandse Strijdkrachten, R1163, as a second family). Kind administrative_control: the Stoottroepen are the combat arm of the BS (a component relationship). organic was considered, but organic relations are excluded from build/command_relations.csv and from who_controls, which is what this pass is meant to answer; administrative_control is the schema class for an administrative superior. HANDOFF describes administrative_control as temporary and ordinarily expecting an end; no end day is invented from the January/May transfers into the Koninklijke landmacht (R1162, month only) or from the 8 August 1945 dissolution of the BS (R1163), so the end stays open_at_last_claim. Start is the dated split (C9386), not the 18 September placement of six Eindhoven companies with XXX Corps (CR1285), when de Jong still called them stoottroepen of the OD. End left open at the last linked claim: the early May 1945 London return (C9388, de Jong pp. 757-758) still reports Stoottroepen (and Bewakingstroepen) as those arms in the liberated south. Lodders and Kraandijk (R1162) date the Limburg transfer into the Koninklijke landmacht in January 1945 and the Brabant transfer in May, after which Commando Zuid was abolished; NIMH (R1163) dates the dissolution of the BS as a whole to 8 August 1945. No end day is invented for this relation from those month-only or later dates. Review (branch small-fixes-1113, 14 November 2026, approved by Scott): old value none, new value this relation.

49th (West Riding) Division under II Canadian Corps on the Nijmegen Island from the end of November 1944, when it took the place of the 50th Division (Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 430: the 50th and 51st Divisions "were also withdrawn into reserve, at the end of November" and their places taken by the 49th and the 51st (Highland); p. 433: the 49th reports dykes blown north of Elst on 2 December, is attacked on 4 December and commands both its own and the Highland Division units on the Island from the morning of the 6th). The start is an inferred value: "the end of November" is read as 30 November and the latest possible start is 2 December, the first day the division is named on the Island. The end, 14 March 1945, is an inferred value: Stacey, p. 545, has the division under I Canadian Corps from midday on 15 March (CR0865), so the earlier attachment cannot run past 14 March; no page read dates the end; the latest row that shows the division at its place under II Canadian Corps is the Ellis Zetten row of 18 January 1945 (C1482), which is why the earliest possible end is 18 January. The division stays assigned to I Corps in the dataset (CR0888); this is a temporary attachment (British Batch 2 follow-up, 28 October 2026).

49th (West Riding) Infantry Division under I Canadian Corps from midday on 15 March 1945, the only division under the corps at first (Stacey p. 545); no end date is given on the pages read (the division was still under the corps in May, p. 614), so the end is unknown. The division stays assigned to XXX Corps in the dataset (CR0076).

50th (Northumbrian) Division under II Canadian Corps in the Nijmegen bridgehead from noon on 9 November 1944, when control of the bridgehead passed to First Canadian Army (Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 428; p. 430 puts the division and the 101st US Airborne Division on the Island with the 2nd and 3rd Canadian Divisions). The end, 29 November, is stated by the row C1541 from two histories and the month is an inferred value: Ellis, vol. II, p. 159, says "On the 29th it was moved back to Belgium, where it was reduced to cadre strength" without naming the month, and Stacey, p. 430, says the division was withdrawn into reserve at the end of November. The division stays assigned to XXX Corps in the dataset (CR0077); this is a temporary attachment (British Batch 2 follow-up, 28 October 2026).

The end, 1 April 1945, is an inferred value stated by the row C1546: MacDonald, ch. 16, p. 357, has the plan of 29 March relieve the corps, its British units passing to the British Second Army, p. 362 has the corps headquarters "shifted to the First Army" in the paragraph that follows the entries of 1 and 2 April, and p. 365 has the corps attack under First Army on 6 April; no page read gives an order or a day, so the day before the start of the First Army relation (CR0922, read as 2 April) is used. note: The US XXI Corps under the French First Army from 23 January 1945: de Lattre, History of the French First Army, p. 359, has Devers telegraph at 03.35 on 23 January that the XXI Corps (Milburn), with its organic elements and the reinforced 75th US Division, is put under the French First Army immediately, and p. 365 has the corps command post set up at Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines on 26 January. Riviera to the Rhine ch. 29 (R425) says only that 'by the end of February all major American participants in the Colmar struggle had returned north, including the XXI Corps', without a day. Wikipedia (R160) and the 71st Infantry Division association narrative (trailblazersww2.org, already weighed as secondary on CR0200) give 16 February 1945 as the return to Seventh Army, with a move to Morhange two days later. That day is not used: the official history gives no day, and the 12th Army Group situation map of 20 February (C5877) still shows the corps headquarters at Sainte-Croix-aux-Mines, next to the 26 January command post, which sits awkwardly with a completed move to Morhange on 18 February. XXI Corps reverted to control of Seventh Army and was given a sector on the left.' It does not give a separate day for the reversion, so 15 February is the earliest date. Three secondary sources give 16 February: Wikipedia (R160: attached to the French First Army from 25 January until 16 February 1945), the trailblazersww2.org XXI Corps history (R1166: 'returned to Seventh Army control on February 16th and moved to Morhange two days later'), and the bigpigeon.us ETO unit subordination page (R1167: French First Army 25 Jan, Seventh Army 16 Feb); they probably share one origin, so they count as one weaker family. The end is therefore between 15 and 16 February 1945 (valid_to_earliest 1945-02-15, valid_to 1945-02-16), the last day of the relation is 15 or 16 February, so it is certain through 15 February and possible on 16 February; neither day is chosen. The official history (Riviera to the Rhine ch. 29, R425) gives no day (end of February, all major American participants returned north) and de Lattre (R686) does not date the end; neither contradicts the range. Not resolved: the 12th Army Group situation map of 20 February (C5877) still shows the corps headquarters at Sainte-Croix-aux-Mines (a 0.3 map row, which can lag the move), whereas the XXI Corps history puts the move to Morhange on 18 February; C5877 is not changed. No new relation: the corps had been assigned to the US Seventh Army and 6th Army Group throughout (CR0201 and CR0200, from 27 December 1944), so the reversion is the end of this operational_control, not a new assignment.
